summary:
Izmit leads internal AI tools for Snowflake's sales organization. Roughly half of Snowflake's ~10,000 employees are revenue-generating reps juggling 15 tools and ~1,000 accounts each. The go-to-market assistant, built on Snowflake Cortex and recently renamed from Snowflake Intelligence to Snowflake Co-work, was launched in September 2024 to democratize data and consolidate tools, with the goal of incremental revenue.

He frames trust as the central problem: free-form chatbots are judged on their first five answers, and winning back a bounced rep costs 10x more than earning them. Before touching the agent, he wrote 150 questions straight from the sales process; the first run scored 50% accuracy, establishing the governing rule that 50 questions at 95% beats 100 at 70%. About 60% of the system's data was added post-launch; the agent now spans 15 semantic views, 85 tables, 3,000 columns, 5-6 MCP connections, and ~20 skills.

Rollout proceeded pilot → 10% beta (~600 users, >70% weekly retention) → GA. At GA, only ~20% of the org had tried the product, so Izmit spends 60-70% of his time on demos, dashboards, and sales-leader sponsorship. Months later, the 'wow factor' collapses and the roadmap must progress through talk-to-data, workflow automation via MCP, hyper-personalization, and team-built skills.

He warns against buying the perfect architecture: his team launched with a 9-page agent instruction managed from a Google Doc, and now 30-40% of work is constant re-architecting for new capabilities like skills, progressive disclosure, user memory, and Slack interfaces. He urges investing in logs, which become a feedback loop that auto-classifies questions, surfaces feature gaps, ingests PRDs from Confluence/Jira, and auto-generates battle cards and matchmakes teams, producing compounding platform value.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and context
sections.summary: Izmit introduces himself as lead for internal AI tools supporting Snowflake's go-to-market team. Notes the assistant launched September 2024, has answered 1M+ questions at ~40K/week, and is built on Snowflake Cortex. He explains to family-and-friends audience why GTM matters: ~half of Snowflake's ~10K employees are revenue-generating reps juggling 15 tools and ~1,000 accounts, making AI-driven data democratization, tool consolidation, and workflow automation a path to incremental revenue.

sections.title: Trust, the 150-question baseline, and 'quality is P minus one'
sections.summary: Izmit argues these projects are non-deterministic and fail on trust, which is hard-earned and lost overnight. Users judge a free-form chatbot on the first five answers, and winning a bounced rep back costs 10x. Before touching the agent, he wrote 150 questions from the sales process; engineering objected the data wasn't connected, but the first run scored 50%, setting the rule: 50 questions at 95% beats 100 at 70%. ~60% of data was added post-launch; the agent now has 15 semantic views, 85 tables, 3,000 columns, 5-6 MCP connections, and ~20 skills.

sections.title: Phased rollout: pilot → 10% beta → GA
sections.summary: Launch is phased to protect the first-five-questions impression. Pilot proves accuracy with eager, AI-native users. 10% beta (~600 users) validates an MVP and surfaces highest-demand data; Izmit gated scale on a >70% weekly retention rate. At GA, only ~20% of the org had tried the product, which Izmit frames as an activation problem, not a technology one.

sections.title: Change management as the real failure mode
sections.summary: Izmit estimates 60-70% of his time goes to sales meetings, demos, adoption dashboards, and getting sponsorship from sales leaders to push adoption. Without this, he claims the assistant would be at roughly half its current adoption. He urges engineers to line up activation and change management with launch, not after.

sections.title: The collapsing wow factor and the talk-to-data → automate → build roadmap
sections.summary: After a few months, the wow factor of talking to data collapses as it becomes baseline habit. Izmit outlines a multi-wave roadmap: (1) talk to your data / data democratization, (2) automate workflows via MCP connections (inbox and Slack monitoring, drafting Gmail responses, outreach automation, turning reps into orchestrators), and (3) team-built tooling and skills, freeing GTM teams from IT backlogs and SaaS-vendor procurement.

sections.title: Hyper-personalization and the cost of standing still
sections.summary: The team-built-skills wave unlocks custom dashboards, deployed applications, automations, and alerts tailored to each team. This leads to a hyper-personalization phase where both the rep and their customers get living context (customers, contacts, etc.). Izmit warns that stopping at the first wave raises expectations, makes it the new baseline, and lets competitors disrupt in 1-2 months because switching is now trivially easy; teams must keep iterating to maintain the wow factor.

sections.title: Don't shop for the perfect architecture; expect constant re-architecting
sections.summary: Large enterprises often stall trying to test frameworks and buy the perfect architecture instead of building and launching. Izmit's team literally launched to 6,000 users with a 9-page agent instruction managed out of a Google Doc plus a couple of Cortex analyst tools, semantic views, and a Cortex search service. Everything in the 'blue boxes' (CI/CD, eval infrastructure, skill library, MCP orchestration, progressive disclosure, user memory, task scheduling, Slack interface) was added after launch. Only ~80% of the original PRD matches today's architecture; 30-40% of current work is re-architecting for new capabilities. He urges teams to run with new tech, avoid over-investing in current architecture, and pivot easily, because waiting 3-4 months behind competitors also means losing customers.

sections.title: Logs as a feedback-loop gold mine
sections.summary: Izmit strongly recommends investing in logs as the feedback loop that compounds platform value. At 1.2M total questions and 40K/week, his team uses LLMs to classify logs into detailed topic/subcategory breakdowns and surfaces real-time feature gaps (questions they can't answer, users swearing or repeating). This replaces interviewing ~100 sellers/week, reveals knowledge-doc/battle-card gaps immediately, and feeds an automated loop: ingest PRDs from Confluence/Jira/Slack, generate battle cards and sales enablement docs, push them back into the agent. Logs also enable cross-team matchmaking (e.g., pinging teams targeting the same accounts from different angles). He frames the pattern as: first features are hard, the next ones are easy, then tapping logs triggers a hockey-stick exponential curve.

sections.title: Closing lessons
sections.summary: Izmit recaps the five takeaways: (1) quality over coverage—going for coverage shoots you in the foot; (2) change management—AI initiatives fail at activation, not technology, especially at 6,000-user scale; (3) collapsing wow factor—don't surf one innovation for a year, be paranoid about the next demo; (4) build fast with today's stack—avoid 6-9 month architecture projects, turn around in days/weeks, and accept constant re-architecting; (5) feedback loops from logs are what produce the incremental hockey-stick value. He notes Snowflake publishes blog posts on agent instructions, semantic views, RAG knowledge assistants, and the non-technical/change-management side.

sections.title: Q&A: Snowflake Intelligence / Co-work as the underlying platform
sections.summary: In Q&A, Izmit clarifies that the internal GTM assistant is built on the platform recently renamed from Snowflake Intelligence to Snowflake Co-work—a no-code agent platform with Cortex analyst, Cortex search, and related tools out of the box. Snowflake was its own customer zero, bringing first- and third-party data (including Salesforce and call transcripts) into Snowflake so agents inherit role-based access controls and can be deployed without code. Customers can build similar agents on the same platform with curated guardrails, and the chat UI is included.
